AI-Assisted NDT Procedure Development: What It Can (and Can't) Do

AI-assisted drafting is a real, growing practice in NDT procedure writing — faster code lookups, faster first-pass drafts. Here's what it genuinely helps with, and what still has to come from a qualified Level III.

By Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III · August 10, 2026

The Real Trend: AI as a Drafting Assistant, Not a Procedure Author of Record

Writing an NDT procedure — a formal document specifying scope, applicable codes, personnel qualifications, equipment, calibration, technique, acceptance criteria, and reporting requirements per ASME Section V Article 1 — is slow, detail-heavy work. It means cross-referencing construction codes (ASME B31.3, B31.4, Section VIII) against the method-specific NDE article, checking client specification overlays (an operator's own SAEP or DEP document), and drafting technique sheets for every weld configuration or component geometry involved. It is exactly the kind of structured, reference-heavy drafting task that large language models are genuinely useful for as a starting point — which is why AI-assisted procedure drafting has become a real, growing practice across the inspection industry, not a hypothetical one.

The honest framing matters here: AI helps a Level III or procedure writer move faster through the drafting process. It does not write an approved, qualified procedure on its own, and no current certification scheme or code lets it try.

Where AI Genuinely Helps Today

  • Faster code and reference lookup: Cross-referencing which ASME Section V clauses a given construction code invokes, or pulling the relevant EN ISO / API cross-reference for a client's dual-scheme requirement, is exactly the kind of retrieval task an LLM can accelerate — provided the output gets checked against the actual current code edition, not assumed correct.
  • First-pass compliance-checklist generation: Turning a construction code's NDE requirements into a checklist of what a procedure needs to cover is a mechanical, structured task AI tools can draft quickly, giving a procedure writer a starting skeleton instead of a blank page.
  • Faster first-draft technique sheets: Drafting the first pass of a technique sheet — wedge selection, frequency, scan pattern — against a known, common weld geometry can move faster with AI assistance, though every parameter still needs verification against the actual component and reference standard.

What Still Has to Come From a Qualified Person

SNT-TC-1A and ASME Section IX both draw a hard line here: a procedure isn't usable on a job until a qualified person has reviewed, qualified, and approved it. For NDT procedures, that means an NDT Level III review and approval. For welding procedure specifications (WPS), it means the procedure qualification record (PQR) process — physically demonstrating on representative production samples that the procedure produces consistent, reproducible results — which is a hands-on validation step no AI tool touches. See Atlantis NDT's technical procedure development methodology for the full seven-step process this actually runs through, from scope and code definition through Level III review to procedure qualification and client submission.

This isn't a temporary limitation waiting on better models. A Level III's approval carries documented accountability under SNT-TC-1A — the same reason, discussed in more depth on our AI in NDT defect detection page, that AI-flagged interpretation results still require human, certified disposition. The pattern is consistent across NDT: AI accelerates the drafting or the first-pass review, a qualified person still owns the sign-off.

Why Every Procedure Still Needs Real Revision Control

Whether a procedure's first draft came from a blank page, a prior revision, or an AI-assisted draft, none of that changes what happens after approval: the procedure has to go under formal document control. That means a locked revision number, an approval history, role-based access so field technicians can only pull the current approved revision, and report numbering that ties every issued inspection report back to the exact procedure revision in effect at the time. This is exactly what Atlantis NDT ERP's document-control module is built to enforce — a procedure can't go live for field use until it carries an approved, current revision status, and every prior revision is archived rather than overwritten so it can be retrieved during an audit. An AI-assisted draft doesn't skip this step; it just changes how the draft got to the review stage.

Where This Leaves NDT Level IIIs and Procedure Writers

The realistic near-term picture for procedure development mirrors what's happening with AI-assisted defect interpretation: a productivity layer for the qualified person, not a replacement for them. The qualification pathway that produces a Level III capable of reviewing and approving a procedure — documented experience, examination, continuing accountability — doesn't change because a first draft got assembled faster.
